summary.text: Sonar is a technique that uses sound, usually underwater, to navigate, measure distances, communicate, or detect objects such as other vessels.
Passive sonar listens for the sounds vessels make, while active sonar sends out pulses of sound and listens for their echoes.
It was developed during World War I to counter the growing threat of submarines, with a working passive system in use by 1918.

items.prompt: A crew switches off everything that makes noise and simply listens through underwater microphones for the engines of other ships. What kind of sonar are they using?

items.prompt: Using sound to echo-locate underwater, the way bats do in the air, seems to have been prompted by which 1912 event?

options.label: The eruption of a volcano at sea
The Titanic striking an iceberg
A submarine sinking a warship
A whale ramming a fishing boat

items.explain: The idea seems to have been prompted by the Titanic disaster of 1912, and the first echo-ranging patent was filed a month after it sank.

items.prompt: In 1914 Fessenden's 500 Hz device detected an iceberg 2 miles away but could not tell which direction it lay in. Why not?

options.label: Its 3-metre wavelength was large for its small face
The iceberg soaked up most of the sound
Cold water bent the sound too much
It could only send Morse code signals

items.explain: With a 3-metre wavelength and a radiating face less than a third of a wavelength across, the device could not determine the iceberg's bearing.

items.prompt: Early ASDIC ships attacked submarines with depth charges rolled off the stern. Why did they lose sonar contact just before the attack?

options.label: The submarine shut its engines and went silent
The ship's own speed drowned out the echoes
Exploding charges deafened the equipment
The ship had to pass over the submarine first

items.explain: To drop charges over the stern, the attacker had to pass over the submerged contact, losing ASDIC contact and firing blind in the final moments.

items.prompt: In the creeping attack, one ship tracked the submarine on ASDIC while a second ship, its ASDIC off, crept in at 5 knots as directed. What did this gain?

options.label: The second ship could not be heard at all
The submarine could not tell when charges would drop
The tracking ship could ram the submarine
Both ships could drop charges at the same time

items.explain: Because the approach was so slow, the submarine could not predict when the attacking ship would release its depth charges.

paragraphs.heading: What sonar is
paragraphs.text: Sonar, short for sound navigation and ranging, is a way of using sound, usually underwater, to find your way, measure distances, communicate, or detect objects such as other ships. The word also names the equipment that makes and receives the sound. There are two kinds. Passive sonar just listens for the noises vessels make, while active sonar sends out pulses of sound and listens for the echoes. The sounds used range from very low (infrasonic) to extremely high (ultrasonic) frequencies.

paragraphs.heading: How active sonar works
paragraphs.text: Modern active sonar uses a device called a transducer to make a sound wave, which bounces back off objects in the water. Sonar can locate these "targets" by sound and measure the character of their echoes. The study of sound under water is called underwater acoustics, or hydroacoustics. The same idea also guides robots, and an upward-looking version used in air, called sodar, helps study the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Early ideas
paragraphs.text: Some animals, including dolphins and bats, have used sound to communicate and find objects for millions of years. The first recorded human use in water was by Leonardo da Vinci in 1490, who reportedly put a tube in the water and listened at it to detect ships. In the late 1800s, underwater bells backed up lighthouses and lightships in warning of hazards. The Titanic disaster of 1912 seems to have prompted the idea of echo-locating underwater the way bats do in air. A month after the sinking, English meteorologist Lewis Fry Richardson filed the first patent anywhere for a device that ranged by underwater echo, and German physicist Alexander Behm patented an echo sounder in 1913.

paragraphs.heading: Finding an iceberg
paragraphs.text: Canadian engineer Reginald Fessenden, working for the Submarine Signal Company in Boston, began building an experimental system in 1912. In a 1914 test from the U.S. Revenue Cutter Miami on the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, he showed it could sound depth, send Morse code underwater, and range by echo, picking up an iceberg 2 miles (3.2 km) away. His "Fessenden oscillator" worked at about 500 Hz. It could not tell which direction the iceberg lay in, because the 3-metre wavelength was large compared with the small radiating face of the transducer.

paragraphs.heading: War and secrecy
paragraphs.text: Sonar grew up in World War I as a response to the rising danger from submarines, and a working passive system was in use by 1918. Early on, the British used hydrophones, devices for listening under water. In 1915 the French physicist Paul Langevin, together with Constantin Chilowsky, worked on active sound devices to find submarines. British work for the Anti-Submarine Division, kept deeply secret, used quartz crystals to make the world's first practical active underwater detector. To hide its purpose the work was called "ASD"ics, which gave the British name ASDIC.

paragraphs.heading: ASDIC at sea
paragraphs.text: In 1939 the Admiralty invented the story that ASDIC stood for "Allied Submarine Detection Investigation Committee", though no such committee has been found in its archives. The British tested ASDIC on HMS Antrim in 1920 and began production in 1922. At first its value was limited by the depth charge: an attacker had to pass over the submarine and drop charges off the stern, losing ASDIC contact just before the attack. In those moments the hunter was firing blind, and the submarine could dodge. New tactics and new weapons fixed this.

paragraphs.heading: The creeping attack
paragraphs.text: One such tactic, the creeping attack, was developed by Frederic John Walker. It used two anti-submarine ships, usually sloops or corvettes. One tracked the submarine with ASDIC and directed the other, which had its own ASDIC switched off and moved in at 5 knots. Because the approach was so slow, the submarine could not tell when the depth charges would fall.
